questions.q: State the SI unit of magnetic dipole moment and write its dimensional formula.
questions.a: SI unit: A·m² (ampere meter squared) or J/T (joule per tesla). Dimensional formula: [𝐿²𝐴]. A wrong answer like “tesla” or “A/m” reveals confusion between magnetic moment and magnetic field or magnetisation.

questions.q: A bar magnet of magnetic moment 0.5 A·m² is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. The magnet’s axis makes an angle of 30° with the field. Calculate the torque on the magnet. Explain why the torque is maximum at 90° and zero at 0°.
questions.a: 𝜏 = 𝑚𝐵 sin𝜃 = (0.5)(0.2) sin30° = 0.1 × 0.5 = 0.05 N·m. Torque is maximum at 90° because sin90° = 1 (lever arm is maximum), zero at 0° because sin0° = 0 (moment aligned with field, no turning effect). If a student uses cos𝜃 or forgets sin𝜃, they confuse torque with potential energy.

questions.q: A closely wound solenoid of 500 turns, cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m², carries a current of 1.5 A. Calculate its magnetic moment. If this solenoid is suspended freely in a uniform horizontal magnetic field of 0.3 T, what is the maximum torque it can experience?
questions.a:
Step 1: 𝑚 = 𝑁𝐼𝐴 = 500 × 1.5 × 2.0×10⁻⁴ = 0.15 A·m².  
Step 2: Maximum torque 𝜏_max = 𝑚𝐵 = 0.15 × 0.3 = 0.045 N·m.  
A wrong answer like 0.15 N·m (forgetting 𝐵) or using 𝑚 = 𝐼𝐴 without 𝑁 reveals misunderstanding of solenoid moment.

questions.q: Compare the potential energy of a magnetic dipole in a uniform field at orientations 𝜃 = 0°, 90°, 180°. Which orientation is stable equilibrium? Which is unstable? Justify using the expression 𝑈 = −𝐦·𝐁.
questions.a: 𝑈(0°) = −𝑚𝐵 (minimum, stable), 𝑈(90°) = 0 (reference), 𝑈(180°) = +𝑚𝐵 (maximum, unstable). Stable equilibrium at 𝜃 = 0° because any small displacement produces a restoring torque. Unstable at 180° because displacement increases misalignment. If a student says 180° is stable, they confuse “aligned” with “anti-aligned.”

questions.q: A student writes: “The magnetic moment of a bar magnet points from its south pole to its north pole.” Evaluate this statement. Is it correct? If not, correct it and explain the convention.
questions.a: Incorrect. By convention, magnetic dipole moment 𝐦 points from south pole to north pole **inside** the magnet, i.e., from geographic south to geographic north when freely suspended. Externally, field lines emerge from north and enter south. The student likely confused the direction of 𝐁 (north to south outside) with 𝐦.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a compass needle, a battery, and a coil of wire to demonstrate that a current loop behaves as a magnetic dipole. Specify how you would determine the direction of its magnetic moment.
questions.a: Wind insulated copper wire (~20 turns) on a cardboard tube. Connect to a 1.5 V cell via a switch. Place a compass at the center of the coil’s axis. Close the switch; compass deflects. Use right-hand rule: curl fingers in current direction, thumb gives 𝐦 direction. Reverse current to see compass flip. A poor answer omits the right-hand rule or uses a straight wire instead of a loop.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Magnetic dipole moment (𝐦) is a vector quantity that ______ the magnetic strength and orientation of a magnet or current loop.
Fill in the blank: Observe a compass needle aligning north-south — it behaves like a ______ dipole in Earth’s field.
What is Magnetic dipole moment (𝐦)? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Magnetic dipole moment (𝐦) is a vector quantity that characterizes the magnetic strength and orientation of a magnet or current loop.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Derive potential energy by integrating torque: 𝑑𝑈 = −𝛕·𝑑𝛉 → 𝑈 = −𝐦·𝐁 (zero at 𝜃 = ______°).
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Magnetic dipole moment (𝐦)?
questions.a: Students often think magnetic moment is a scalar because its magnitude 𝑚 = 𝐼𝐴 looks like a scalar product.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can (1) compute magnetic moment of a current loop/solenoid from given 𝐼, 𝑁, 𝐴 with correct units and direction, (2) calculate torque and potential energy of a magnetic dipole in a uniform field using vector cross/dot products, and (3) explain the electrostatic analogy by mapping 𝐩 ↔ 𝐦, 𝐄 ↔ 𝐁, 1/4𝜋𝜀₀ ↔ 𝜇₀/4𝜋.
